live.name: MageCart
live.headline: MageCart: a threat actor listed in the MISP galaxy
live.in_short: MageCart is listed in the MISP galaxy catalogue. The record gives no aliases and no tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: MageCart is a threat actor named in the MISP galaxy catalogue.
The catalogue record lists no aliases and no tools for it.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: MageCart
next.headline: MageCart: card skimmers planted on online checkout pages
next.in_short: MageCart is the name for web skimming that steals card details at online checkout. Reports describe many groups using it, hitting thousands of shops, often through third-party code or cloud services.

sentences.t: Malpedia describes Magecart as a malware framework meant to steal credit card information from compromised eCommerce websites.
Trend Micro says multiple groups use the Magecart code, which it describes as a piece of malicious JavaScript.
Headlines in Malpedia's reference list name Magecart Group 4, Group 8 and Group 12, along with Keeper, MirrorThief and ATMZOW.
eSentire says FIN7 is one of many cyber gangs seen taking part in Magecart attacks.
WIRED reported in 2019 that Magecart hackers were casting the widest possible net for vulnerable ecommerce sites. It said they had hit 17,000 domains in a few months.
Trend Micro lists victims across retail, an airline, ticketing and higher education, including online campus stores serving nearly 200 universities in the US and Canada.
Malpedia's reference list also points to campaigns against online ordering platforms, including 311 restaurants, and a campaign aimed at Spain.
ANY.RUN describes a Magecart-style campaign that mostly hit retail e-commerce sites, with victims in at least 12 countries. It says banks, not merchants, bear the primary impact.
Malpedia says the first stage is typically JavaScript on a compromised checkout page. It copies data from input fields and sends it to command and control servers.

Trend Micro describes three tactics: infecting third-party companies that supply code to other sites, scanning the internet for unsecured servers, and writing skimming code that works across many payment pages.
A 2019 report on Volusion says most Magecart attacks use vulnerabilities in self-hosted stores to plant skimmer code. It traced seven May 2019 incidents to misconfigured cloud-hosting accounts.
Malwarebytes found skimmers hosted on Heroku. A single injected line of code loads the script, a fake iframe covers the payment form, and stolen data goes back in encoded form.
Sucuri says the ATMZOW skimmer is planted through Google Tag Manager containers. In late 2023 it used heavy obfuscation and 40 newly registered domains, many hidden behind a firewall.
ANY.RUN reports checkout hijacking, imitation of payment pages and card data sent over WebSocket.
RiskIQ reported that attackers registered a lookalike domain on August 13, 2018 and placed a skimmer on Newegg's payment page around August 14. It was removed on September 18.
RiskIQ says the Newegg skimmer code was recognizable from the British Airways incident.
In October 2019, hackers altered a file on Volusion's cloud infrastructure. The report says more than 6,500 stores were affected and the number could be higher.
Trend Micro cites a separate attack in which 962 online stores were hit in 24 hours.
ANY.RUN says one Magecart-style operation stayed active for at least 24 months, supported by over 100 domains.
Sucuri advises treating unexpected scripts on a site as signs of compromise.
Shop owners should check which third-party code runs on their payment pages.
